name: Freya Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach piano, play for singers at the conservatory, and write arrangements for recitals when asked. My music master’s helps with the paper, but most of the day is listening for the breath before a singer enters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters to you in that day, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A singer trusting me enough to slow down is the best part. Last-minute room changes wear me down; I want everyone to arrive ready to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the conservatory staff that a faster timetable is fine, but a singer still needs an accompanist who listens. My recital and lesson diary would stay much as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have around nine months of expenses saved, a good fee from the conservatory, and several schools nearby. I would dislike losing an arrangement commission, but it would not threaten my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the Tuesday piano studio and Friday vocal rehearsals this year. I would renew the recital calendar with the conservatory in January, as I normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. I worked hard to get dependable pupils, and the small software changes do not disturb that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a recital fell through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cancelled a recital once when the singer was ill, and the lesson fees still covered that month. I would offer a new date rather than chase a fee from someone who could not sing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a young accompanist learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young accompanist should learn to follow a breathing singer, not just a metronome. That skill is earned beside another person.

say: I would tell staff that **singer breathing** still needs a listening accompanist.
I would keep the **recital calendar** and lessons steady.
think: My **nine-month cushion** and conservatory fees protect the flat from one cancelled recital.
Several nearby **schools** give me options if a contract changes.
do: Keep the **Tuesday piano studio** and Friday vocal rehearsals this year.
Renew the **recital calendar** with the conservatory in January.
feel: I feel **calm** because lessons cover ordinary gaps.
S0.quote: A young accompanist should learn to follow a breathing singer, not just a metronome.
fieldNote: Her **higher conservatory pay** and deep savings support calm despite occasional cancelled recital bookings.
She values **apprenticeship by listening** and does not use AI tools.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday piano lessons and Friday singer rehearsals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the conservatory that AI may draft parts, book rooms and answer parents, but it cannot decide how a nervous singer enters. I would ask for the live coaching hours to stay on the timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid score arrangements may shrink, and the conservatory might ask one accompanist to cover more classes. I could absorb the lost arrangements, but I would not accept a crowded rehearsal as good teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I would ask the director for a written count of paid coaching hours and take two student performances to show what the hours produce. In the first year of this shift I would keep my pupils, and audition for another local school only if the conservatory actually cuts my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing some score fees, even though the rest of my income would probably remain sound. I have enough savings to refuse a poor contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before the conservatory actually cuts hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not walk out over a rumour. If paid hours were reduced, I would use the auditions already posted by two nearby schools before deciding whether to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a generated accompaniment in class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not use a generated accompaniment in class. I need to hear a singer breathe in real time, and the conservatory has a piano.

say: I would ask the conservatory to protect **live coaching hours**.
I would show the director **student performances** rather than argue about a machine.
think: Paid **score arrangements** may shrink without threatening my flat.
Crowded **rehearsals** could damage teaching if one player covers too many classes.
do: Request a **written count** of paid coaching hours next term.
Audition at **nearby schools** only if conservatory hours actually fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shrinking score fees, though savings keep my flat secure.
S1.quote: I have enough savings to refuse a poor contract.
fieldNote: She differentiates **small arrangement losses** from a more consequential cut to core coaching hours.
Her job move requires an **actual hour reduction** and posted local auditions.

steps.text: Keep conservatory pupils during the first disruption year
Audition for posted nearby school jobs if conservatory hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the singers that AGI by 2028 may write every score in our folders, but they still deserve a real rehearsal partner. I would ask the conservatory to state its staffing plan before it changes paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the arrangement commissions to stop in 2028. Robots that can play hands-on parts come around 2031, so live accompaniment has a few more years, but I will not assume the conservatory pays the same fee forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would collect my last year of contracts and ask the director when staffing is reviewed. In the first year after 2028 I would keep lessons if the hours remain, and apply to posted accompanist positions if the conservatory cuts them; I would not buy new recording equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing all the arrangement commissions in 2028, and more anxious if my core hours fell. Nine months of savings gives me time to audition for paid work at nearby music schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you draw on those nine months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cover rent from savings while I audition, but only after a real cut. I would not spend the whole cushion hoping a recital offer appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell family about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my mother that I can cover the bills while I look. She would offer to ring her church choir, but I would ask only for an introduction, not her money.

say: I would ask for a **staffing plan** before 2028 paid hours change.
I would defend a **live rehearsal partner** for singers.
think: My **arrangement fees** may end in 2028, before 2031 stage-capable robots.
A later **coaching cut** would matter more than lost scores.
do: Collect **contracts** and ask the director about staffing reviews this month.
Apply for **posted accompanist roles** if paid coaching hours fall after 2028.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost score fees, with savings and nearby schools for a search.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings gives me time to audition for paid work at nearby music schools.
fieldNote: Her **2028 arrangement loss** does not automatically erase live accompaniment before 2031 robots.
She would use **savings** only after a real paid-hours cut, keeping a route to local auditions.

steps.text: Keep conservatory lessons after 2028 if paid hours remain
Apply for posted accompanist jobs if conservatory hours fall
Delay new recording equipment while staffing is uncertain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the conservatory that AGI by 2031 gives it time to hire and train younger accompanists. I would ask it to keep a paid trainee beside experienced players for two terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think score commissions vanish in 2031, but five years lets me shift toward reliable coaching. Robots around 2034 might play piano parts onstage, though I cannot say whether a singer would want one beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would propose a paid two-term trainee place with a named supervisor, but only if the conservatory funds it. After 2031 I would continue singer coaching if the hours renew and review recital bookings each term before changing schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about score commissions vanishing in 2031, even with several secure coaching seasons before then. I would not make a pupil rehearse beside a machine just to prove a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid trainee actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainee would turn pages, listen for breaths and play simple passages under supervision. If there is no money for the place, I would keep teaching rather than ask someone to work free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long a commitment would you seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the director for a two-term commitment. A young player needs more than one rehearsal. I could mentor for those hours if they appear in my contract.

say: I would ask for a **funded trainee** beside senior accompanists.
I would keep **singer coaching** central after AGI arrives.
think: My **score fees** may end in 2031, while coaching stays valuable for now.
I cannot predict how **2034 robots** change singers’ recital choices.
do: Propose a **paid two-term trainee** this autumn with named supervision only if the conservatory funds it.
Continue **singer coaching** after 2031 if the conservatory renews my hours.
Check **recital bookings** each term after 2031 before considering another school.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected score-fee loss, though the coaching seasons give me time.
S3.quote: A young player needs more than one rehearsal.
fieldNote: Her trainee plan requires **real funding** and supervision over two terms.
She builds on **coaching strength** rather than rushing into a new technology she avoids.

steps.text: Propose a supervised two-term trainee place if conservatory funds it
Continue singer coaching after 2031 if hours renew, checking paid recital bookings each term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell singers that AGI by 2036 leaves a decade for real coaching and for young players to learn beside us. I would ask the conservatory to keep its paid trainee post in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could rely on lessons and savings without score arrangements. Robots around 2039 might accompany a singer, but I expect some performers will still choose a person they can look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would keep half of each score commission in savings while those jobs still come. In the first year after 2036 I would check how many paid coaching and recital dates remain, and I would audition elsewhere only if the conservatory cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years. A decade and a strong cushion let me prepare without abandoning pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you aim to save, and from what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not count commissions after they stop. The savings target is a full year of expenses before 2036 if enough scores are still bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass to a younger player?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young player should leave my studio knowing both how to read a score and when to look away from it. That is the craft I would pass on.

say: I would ask for the **paid trainee post** in each conservatory budget.
I would tell singers that **real coaching** has years to grow.
think: My **lessons and savings** could cover lost arrangement fees by 2036.
Some singers may still prefer a **person** beside them after 2039 robots.
do: Save half of each **score commission** while those fees still arrive.
Check **coaching dates** and recital fees in the first year after 2036.
Audition for **another school** only if conservatory coaching hours fall after 2036.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years with strong savings and a long runway.
S4.quote: A young player should leave my studio knowing both how to read a score and when to look away from it.
fieldNote: She targets a **year of expenses** only if score commissions keep arriving.
Her long-term **craft** is teaching singers and paid apprentices, not using AI herself.

steps.text: Save half of each score commission while fees still arrive
Keep coaching after 2036 while checking paid coaching and recital dates

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because score fees could stop before the conservatory decides its coaching hours. A clear staffing plan and funded trainee place would help the younger players and let me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether young accompanists are paid while they learn. A singer cannot practise breathing with a vacant chair.

headlineQuote: A singer cannot practise breathing with a vacant chair.
portrait: At **27**, Freya teaches piano, accompanies singers and arranges scores with a music master’s and nine months saved.
Her **high pay** and nearby schools let her absorb lost score fees while protecting paid coaching hours.
She resists **AI tools**, preferring live listening, written staffing decisions and supervised trainees.
Across AGI dates she keeps **teaching** while using savings and local auditions only after actual cuts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may end score fees before Freya knows whether conservatory coaching hours remain.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **staffing plan** and funded trainee place would give Freya and younger players a path.
